title: Networks, the Internet, and Cybersecurity Essentials
objective: Analyze how networks transmit data and apply cybersecurity principles to identify and mitigate common digital threats.
body:
A **computer network** is a collection of devices connected together to share resources and communicate. Networks are classified by size and scope: a **LAN (Local Area Network)** covers a small area such as a home or office, while a **WAN (Wide Area Network)** spans large geographic distances. The **internet** is the world's largest WAN — a global network of networks interconnected through standardized protocols.

Communication across networks depends on agreed-upon rules called **protocols**. The foundational protocol suite is **TCP/IP (Transmission Control Protocol / Internet Protocol)**. **IP** assigns a unique numerical address to every device on a network, allowing data to be routed to the correct destination. **TCP** ensures reliable delivery by breaking data into **packets**, sending them independently across the network, and reassembling them in the correct order at the destination. The **HTTP** and **HTTPS** protocols govern how web browsers request and receive web pages, with HTTPS adding encryption for security.

Network hardware includes **routers**, which direct packets between different networks; **switches**, which connect devices within the same network; and **access points**, which provide wireless (**Wi-Fi**) connectivity. Every network device has a **MAC address** — a unique hardware identifier burned into its network interface card — while **IP addresses** are logical addresses assigned by network configuration.

Cybersecurity protects digital systems from unauthorized access, damage, and theft. The **CIA triad** — **Confidentiality**, **Integrity**, and **Availability** — represents the three core goals of information security. **Confidentiality** means only authorized users access data; **Integrity** means data is accurate and unaltered; **Availability** means systems and data are accessible when needed.

Common threats include **malware** (malicious software), which encompasses **viruses** (self-replicating programs), **ransomware** (encrypts files and demands payment), **spyware** (secretly monitors users), and **Trojans** (malware disguised as legitimate software). **Phishing** is a social engineering attack where attackers impersonate trusted entities via email or websites to steal credentials. Defenses include **firewalls** (filter incoming/outgoing network traffic), **encryption** (scrambles data so only authorized parties can read it), **multi-factor authentication (MFA)** (requires two or more verification methods), and regular **software updates** to patch known vulnerabilities.
examples: When you check your bank balance online, HTTPS encrypts the connection between your browser and the bank's server — without it, anyone on the same Wi-Fi could intercept your account credentials in plain text.

A ransomware attack on a hospital encrypts patient records and demands $500,000 for the decryption key, directly violating the Availability principle of the CIA triad by making critical data inaccessible.

A home router acts as both a router (directing traffic between your LAN and the internet WAN) and a switch (connecting your devices to each other) — illustrating how consumer devices often combine network functions.

questions.stem: A company's database is altered without authorization, changing employee salary records. Which CIA triad principle has been violated?
questions.explanation: Integrity ensures data remains accurate and unaltered by unauthorized parties. Confidentiality would be violated if unauthorized users merely viewed the records without changing them.

questions.stem: Which protocol is responsible for breaking data into packets and ensuring they are reassembled correctly at the destination?
questions.explanation: TCP (Transmission Control Protocol) handles reliable delivery by sequencing packets and requesting retransmission of lost ones. IP handles addressing and routing, not sequencing or error correction.

questions.stem: An employee receives an email appearing to be from IT support asking them to confirm their password. This attack is best described as:
questions.explanation: Phishing impersonates trusted entities to trick users into revealing credentials. Ransomware encrypts files and demands payment — it does not typically involve fake emails requesting passwords.

questions.stem: What distinguishes a router from a switch in a typical office network?
choices: A router connects devices wirelessly; a switch uses only wired connections
A router directs traffic between different networks; a switch connects devices within the same network
A router stores MAC addresses; a switch stores IP addresses
A router provides power over Ethernet; a switch does not
questions.explanation: Routers operate at the network layer and forward packets between different networks (e.g., LAN to internet). Switches operate at the data link layer connecting devices within a single LAN using MAC addresses.

questions.stem: A user enables two-factor authentication on their email account. This security measure is best described as:
choices: A firewall rule blocking external access
Requiring two verification methods before granting access
Automatic malware scanning of incoming attachments
questions.explanation: Multi-factor authentication (MFA) requires users to provide two or more forms of verification (e.g., password plus a phone code). A firewall controls network traffic but does not verify individual user identities.

questions.stem: Malware that disguises itself as a helpful free utility but secretly gives an attacker remote access to the system is classified as a:
questions.explanation: A Trojan (Trojan horse) disguises itself as legitimate software to deceive users into installing it. A virus self-replicates by attaching to other files, which a Trojan does not necessarily do.

questions.stem: Which of the following best explains why HTTPS is preferred over HTTP for online shopping?
choices: HTTPS loads pages faster than HTTP
HTTPS encrypts data in transit, protecting payment information from interception
HTTPS prevents the website from collecting cookies
HTTPS guarantees the website has no malware
questions.explanation: HTTPS uses TLS encryption to secure data between the browser and server, preventing interception of sensitive data like credit card numbers. Page speed depends on many factors beyond the protocol.

questions.stem: A network covers an entire college campus connecting multiple buildings. This is most accurately classified as:
questions.explanation: A LAN covers a single building or a campus-sized area, even one with several buildings. A MAN spans a city or metropolitan area, and a WAN spans cities, countries or global distances.

flashcards.definition: The foundational protocol suite of the internet, where IP handles device addressing and routing while TCP ensures reliable, ordered delivery of data packets.
The three core principles of information security: Confidentiality (only authorized access), Integrity (data accuracy), and Availability (systems accessible when needed).
A network security system that monitors and filters incoming and outgoing network traffic based on predefined security rules to block unauthorized access.
A social engineering cyberattack in which an attacker impersonates a trusted entity through email or fake websites to trick users into revealing sensitive information.
The process of converting readable data into an unreadable coded format so that only parties with the correct decryption key can access the original information.
